title: 2027 Grammy Snubs and Surprises: Madonna, Noah Kahan, Audrey Hobert and More
summary: Madonna and Kahan were locked out of nominations in the top categories, the Womack Sisters were recognized and country’s gender divide showed up in an unexpected way.

## Most Surprising Song Pick: Rosalía’s ‘Berghain’


There’s an arty wild-card in the top Grammy categories. Rosalía’s 2025 album “Lux (Complete Works)” is nominated for album of the year; its track “Berghain” is up for song and record of the year. “Lux (Complete Works),” which was[just named album of the year](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/arts/music/rosalia-milo-j-latin-grammys-winners.html) at the Latin Grammys, has lyrics in more than a dozen languages, a panoply of collaborators and arrangements that encompass orchestras, electronics and flamenco. Although “Berghain” is named after Berlin’s renowned dance club, its music is full-tilt operatic, with Rosalía backed by an orchestra and choir; she sings in German and Spanish and shares the track with Björk, who invokes “divine intervention,” and Yves Tumor, whose lyric would have to be bleeped on ABC. Rosalía’s nominations also include nods for other “Lux” songs that are closer to pop: “Sauvignon Blanc” (pop solo performance) and “La Perla” (Latin song). Alongside the pop hits that share the top categories, “Berghain” arrives from an alternate universe. — JON PARELES


## A Letdown for Madonna


Madonna’s 2025 album, “Confessions II,” was widely hailed as a high-concept sequel to her 2005 “Confessions on a Dance Floor” — a major statement after years of uneven albums. “Confessions II” is[a loving, history-minded survey of club culture](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/06/arts/music/madonna-confessions-ii-album-review.html) from someone who’s seen — and changed — it all. But the album was shut out of the top categories, and it doesn’t even get a chance at pop vocal album. “Bring Your Love,” shared with Sabrina Carpenter, is among the nominees for pop duo/group performance, but other “Confessions” tracks are relegated to the dance/electronic categories, which don’t usually appear in prime time. — PARELES


## Most Surprising Nomination Magnet: Angine de Poitrine


The Canadian bass-and-drums duo Angine de Poitrine didn’t exactly scream “Grammy bait” when their[performance on KEXP](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0Ssi-9wS1so&t=9s) went viral earlier this year. Wearing polka-dot costumes with bizarre, face-covering headgear, they looked like errant kids’ TV characters — at least until they laid into their stuttering, microtonal prog grooves. But Angine de Poitrine, up for best new artist and three other awards, captivated the not-so-small sliver of the music world that luxuriates in stuff like this, and nowadays also cherishes it as a kind of oddball antidote to A.I. slop. We used to think of the “real musicianship” contingent of Grammy voters as people who relished a really smooth jazz solo. Maybe this is a new acid test? — BEN SISARIO

## Most Surprising Genre Gender Split: Country Albums


When the Grammys split the best country album category last year into traditional and contemporary branches, the hot take was that it was a reactionary response to Beyoncé winning with “Cowboy Carter” in 2025. And perhaps it was. But did anyone expect it would end up as a gender divide? In its second year, the contemporary country album ballot is all women: Ella Langley, Kacey Musgraves, Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith and Megan Moroney (average age: 31). Traditional country album, on the other hand, is all men: Willie Nelson, Vince Gill, Cody Johnson, Charley Crockett and Charlie Worsham (average age: 57). Hey boys, try something contemporary. — SISARIO
